items.explain: The person's unpaid shelving work at the library becomes a named volunteer role, with a set chair and a weekly visiting companion.

items.plain: Keeps in touch with family online
items.explain: They keep contacting family only by library email, refusing money offered, and are not expected to leave the city.

items.plain: Rushed to clinic with dangerous blood pressure
items.explain: The person suffers a blood pressure emergency needing urgent clinic care, made less likely by repeat prescriptions and monthly checks at the library.

items.plain: Catches chest infection from sick man
items.explain: They catch a lung infection from a seriously ill man sharing the library, a risk reduced by separating their computer times.
The person is moved into long-term supported housing for over-65s instead of getting a council flat; the housing application lapses unresolved.
A concern sent to children's services is closed without a home visit; the family stays together and the person never learns of it.
Benefit penalties stop and appointments fit school hours, but everything goes through one caseworker and the person stops trying to appeal decisions.

items.plain: Stuck in poorly paid care job
items.explain: They stay on insecure, low-paid care work without paid travel, getting slightly steadier hours but remaining on a low income.
Years of lifting in home care cause lasting injury, so the person works less and moves onto sickness benefits managed by a caseworker.

items.plain: Takes sideways job with pay rise
items.explain: The person accepts a same-level supervisory job with a retention bonus, while that area is being automated over the next years.
They stay at the company thanks to a confirmed pay rise and health support, performing steadily but never promoted, with workplace rivalry quiet.
Heavy drinking, untreated high blood pressure and insomnia cause a health crisis and time off sick, less likely if they attend the clinic.
The person's scheduling job is taken over by a computer forecasting system, and they leave with an improved redundancy payout.
They live alone in a smaller home with less income, see mostly their daughter, and only sometimes manage heart health.
At the station the person phones their father rather than leaving, delaying departure by a few days amid family troubles.
They enrol on a social work degree at university, with a $600 transfer from their father covering initial costs.
Through coursework the person formally looks into how the city's housing waiting list decides who gets homes, using a known case.
They qualify in social work and look for a first job; jobs near university are encouraged, home-city applications slowed down.
The person applies for social work in a poor area back home, but it is held up, so they keep their current job.
They settle permanently elsewhere, returning only to visit their father, and gradually disappear from the city's records.
